claim: Ring-forming AAA+ chaperones exert ATP-fueled substrate unfolding by threading through a central pore.
source: Ring-forming AAA+ chaperones exert ATP-fueled substrate unfolding by threading through a central pore.
evidence: This is a statement of established knowledge about AAA+ chaperone mechanism presented in the abstract.

claim: The AAA+ chaperone ClpC with the peptidase ClpP forms a bacterial protease essential to virulence and stress resistance.
source: The AAA+ chaperone ClpC with the peptidase ClpP forms a bacterial protease essential to virulence and stress resistance.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations in the introduction section referencing prior work.

claim: The adaptor MecA activates ClpC by targeting substrates and stimulating ClpC ATPase activity.
source: The adaptor MecA activates ClpC by targeting substrates and stimulating ClpC ATPase activity.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in the manuscript and citations to prior work.

claim: ClpC forms large two-helical assemblies that associate via head-to-head contacts between coiled-coil middle domains (MDs).
source: ClpC forms large two-helical assemblies that associate via head-to-head contacts between coiled-coil middle domains (MDs).
evidence: This is directly supported by cryo-EM structural data presented in Figure 3 and related text.

claim: MecA converts the ClpC resting state to an active planar ring structure by binding to MD interaction sites.
source: MecA converts this resting state to an active planar ring structure by binding to MD interaction sites.
evidence: This is supported by cryo-EM structures of ClpC with and without MecA shown in Figure 3.

claim: Loss of ClpC repression in MD mutants causes constitutive activation and severe cellular toxicity.
source: Loss of ClpC repression in MD mutants causes constitutive activation and severe cellular toxicity.
evidence: This is supported by biochemical assays in Figures 1-2 and cellular toxicity data in Figure 6.

claim: AAA+ proteins control a multitude of essential cellular activities by converting the energy derived from ATP hydrolysis into a mechanical force to remodel bound substrates.
source: AAA+ (ATPase associated with a variety of cellular activities) proteins control a multitude of essential cellular activities by converting the energy derived from ATP hydrolysis into a mechanical force to remodel bound substrates (Hanson and Whiteheart, 2005).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation to Hanson and Whiteheart, 2005.

claim: ClpB/Hsp104 reactivates aggregated proteins in concert with a cognate Hsp70 system.
source: ClpB/Hsp104 reactivates aggregated proteins in concert with a cognate Hsp70 system (Doyle et al., 2013; Mogk et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Doyle et al., 2013 and Mogk et al., 2015.

claim: Loss of control mechanisms of AAA+ protein activity in mutant proteins can lead to cell death.
source: Accordingly, loss of the control mechanisms of AAA+ protein activity in mutant proteins can lead to cell death (Oguchi et al., 2012; Schirmer et al., 2004; Lipińska et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Oguchi et al., 2012; Schirmer et al., 2004; Lipińska et al., 2013.

claim: In the ClpB/Hsp104 disaggregase a long coiled-coil middle domain (MD) forms a repressing belt around the AAA ring to reduce ATPase activity.
source: In the ClpB/Hsp104 disaggregase a long coiled-coil middle domain (MD), consisting of two wings, is forming a repressing belt around the AAA ring to reduce ATPase activity (Carroni et al., 2014; Heuck et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Carroni et al., 2014 and Heuck et al., 2016.

claim: Adjacent MDs in ClpB/Hsp104 bind to each other by head-to-tail interactions keeping the regulatory domains in place.
source: Adjacent MDs bind to each other by head-to-tail interactions keeping the regulatory domains in place.
evidence: This is based on prior structural knowledge of ClpB/Hsp104.

claim: ATPase repression in ClpB/Hsp104 is relieved by MD dissociation and binding to Hsp70 adaptors that prevent reassociation of MDs with the ClpB/Hsp104 ring.
source: ATPase repression is relieved by MD dissociation and binding to Hsp70 adaptors that prevent reassociation of MDs with the ClpB/Hsp104 ring (Oguchi et al., 2012; Rosenzweig et al., 2013; Lee et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Oguchi et al., 2012; Rosenzweig et al., 2013; Lee et al., 2013.

claim: The ClpC-ClpP machinery is crucial for bacterial stress resistance and virulence.
source: The ClpC-ClpP machinery acts in regulatory and general proteolysis, controlling multiple cellular pathways and differentiation processes and is crucial for bacterial stress resistance and virulence (Turgay et al., 1997; Frees et al., 2014; Trentini et al., 2016; Capestany et al., 2008; Msadek et al., 1994; Krüger et al., 1994; Krüger et al., 2000; Lourdault et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior work.

claim: ClpC activity crucially relies on cooperation with adaptor proteins including MecA.
source: ClpC activity crucially relies on cooperation with adaptor proteins including MecA, that target specific substrates while concurrently stimulating ClpC ATPase activity (Schlothauer et al., 2003; Turgay et al., 1997; Mei et al., 2009; Turgay et al., 1998).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Schlothauer et al., 2003; Turgay et al., 1997; Mei et al., 2009; Turgay et al., 1998.

claim: MecA binds to N-terminal and middle domains of each ClpC subunit forming a separate layer on top of the ClpC AAA ring.
source: MecA binds to N-terminal and middle domains of each ClpC subunit forming a separate layer on top of the ClpC AAA ring (Wang et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Wang et al., 2011.

claim: ClpC harbors a coiled-coil MD consisting only of a single wing, as opposed to the two-wing MD of ClpB/Hsp104.
source: Furthermore, ClpC harbors a coiled-coil MD consisting only of a single wing, as opposed to the two-wing MD of ClpB/Hsp104.
evidence: This is a structural comparison based on known domain architectures.

claim: ADEP-activated ClpP causes aberrant protein degradation and allows for eradication of Staphylococcus aureus persister cells.
source: ADEP-activated ClpP causes aberrant protein degradation and even allows for eradication of Staphylococcus aureus persister cells (Conlon et al., 2013; Brötz-Oesterhelt et al., 2005; Kirstein et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Conlon et al., 2013; Brötz-Oesterhelt et al., 2005; Kirstein et al., 2009.

claim: S. aureus ClpC/ClpP exhibits high proteolytic activity in presence of the adaptor MecA.
source: To study the function of the M-domain (MD) in ClpC activity control we first purified S. aureus ClpC/ClpP and demonstrated functionality by determining high-proteolytic activity in presence of the adaptor MecA (Figure 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1.

claim: ClpC wild type together with ClpP exhibited only a low proteolytic activity in absence of MecA.
source: ClpC wild type (WT) together with ClpP exhibited only a low proteolytic activity in absence of MecA and FITC-casein degradation rates were 20-fold increased upon adaptor addition.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A/B.

claim: FITC-casein degradation rates were 20-fold increased upon MecA addition to ClpC wild type.
source: ClpC wild type (WT) together with ClpP exhibited only a low proteolytic activity in absence of MecA and FITC-casein degradation rates were 20-fold increased upon adaptor addition.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A/B.

claim: Most ClpC MD mutants enabled adaptor-independent FITC-casein proteolysis to varying degrees.
source: In contrast, most MD mutants enabled for adaptor-independent FITC-casein proteolysis to varying degrees.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A/B.

claim: ClpC-F436A, ClpC-R443A and ClpC-D444A showed highest activities with degradation rates close to those determined for ClpC WT plus MecA.
source: ClpC-F436A, ClpC-R443A and ClpC-D444A showed highest activities with degradation rates close to those determined for ClpC WT plus MecA (Figure 1A/B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A/B.

claim: MD deletion strongly increased ClpC activity.
source: Similarly, MD deletion strongly increased ClpC activity, indicating that the single point mutants reflect a loss of M-domain function.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A/B.

claim: MecA presence still stimulated FITC-casein degradation by ClpC MD mutants except F436A and ΔM.
source: MecA presence still stimulated FITC-casein degradation by ClpC MD mutants except F436A and ΔM, consistent with the crucial function of F436 in MecA binding (Figure 1A) (Wang et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figure 1A and citation to Wang et al., 2011.

claim: F436 is crucial for MecA binding.
source: MecA presence still stimulated FITC-casein degradation by ClpC MD mutants except F436A and ΔM, consistent with the crucial function of F436 in MecA binding (Figure 1A) (Wang et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Wang et al., 2011 and experimental data.

claim: ClpC-F436A degraded FITC-casein with similar efficiencies as ClpC/MecA at all substrate concentrations tested and reached identical vmax.
source: ClpC-F436A degraded FITC-casein with similar efficiencies as ClpC/MecA at all substrate concentrations tested and reached identical vmax.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B/C.

claim: ClpC-R443A and ClpC-ΔM also degraded FITC-casein at saturating concentrations like MecA-activated ClpC.
source: ClpC-R443A and ClpC-ΔM also degraded FITC-casein at saturating concentrations like MecA-activiated ClpC, underlining complete activation of ClpC upon M-domain mutation (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C)
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C.

claim: ClpC WT/ClpP efficiently degraded GFP-SsrA in a MecA-dependent manner.
source: ClpC WT/ClpP efficiently degraded GFP-SsrA in a MecA-dependent manner (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: ClpC MD mutants did hardly exhibit autonomous degradation of GFP-SsrA in contrast to FITC-casein.
source: Surprisingly, ClpC MD mutants did hardly exhibit autonomous degradation of GFP-SsrA in contrast to FITC-casein.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: GFP-SsrA remained stable in presence of ΔN-ClpC/ClpP.
source: GFP-SsrA remained stable in presence of ΔN-ClpC/ClpP, however, the substrate was rapidly degraded by ΔN-ClpC-F436A, ΔN-ClpC-R443A and ΔN-ClpC-ΔM (+ClpP) and degradation rates were identical to those determined for ClpC WT/ClpP with MecA (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D/E.

claim: GFP-SsrA was rapidly degraded by ΔN-ClpC-F436A, ΔN-ClpC-R443A and ΔN-ClpC-ΔM (+ClpP) with degradation rates identical to those determined for ClpC WT/ClpP with MecA.
source: GFP-SsrA remained stable in presence of ΔN-ClpC/ClpP, however, the substrate was rapidly degraded by ΔN-ClpC-F436A, ΔN-ClpC-R443A and ΔN-ClpC-ΔM (+ClpP) and degradation rates were identical to those determined for ClpC WT/ClpP with MecA (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: The N-domain is essential for MecA binding.
source: We did not test for GFP-SsrA degradation by ΔN-ClpC/ClpP in presence of MecA, as the N-domain is essential for MecA binding (Wang et al., 2011; Kirstein et al., 2006; Persuh et al., 1999).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Wang et al., 2011; Kirstein et al., 2006; Persuh et al., 1999.

claim: ΔN-ClpC-F436A is as active as MecA-activated ClpC and degraded GFP-SsrA with similar or even faster kinetics.
source: By determining GFP-SsrA degradation rates under saturating conditions we confirmed that ΔN-ClpC-F436A is as active as MecA-activated ClpC and degraded the substrate with similar or even faster kinetics (Figure 1—figure supplement 3B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3B.

claim: GFP-SsrA degradation by activated ΔN-ClpC M-domain mutants relied on ATP hydrolysis.
source: GFP-SsrA degradation by activated ΔN-ClpC M-domain mutants relied on ATP hydrolysis and remained specific as the substrate variant GFP-SsrA-DD was not degraded (Figure 1—figure supplement 3D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3D.

claim: The substrate variant GFP-SsrA-DD was not degraded by activated ΔN-ClpC M-domain mutants.
source: GFP-SsrA degradation by activated ΔN-ClpC M-domain mutants relied on ATP hydrolysis and remained specific as the substrate variant GFP-SsrA-DD was not degraded (Figure 1—figure supplement 3D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3D.

claim: In GFP-SsrA-DD, the two C-terminal alanine residues of the SsrA tag are replaced by aspartate residues, obstructing binding to the AAA+ chaperone pore site.
source: Here, the two C-terminal alanine residues of the SsrA tag are replaced by aspartate residues, obstructing binding to the AAA+ chaperone pore site (Flynn et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Flynn et al., 2001.

claim: MD mutations boost ClpC unfolding activity in absence of adaptor without altering general substrate specificity.
source: This documents that MD mutations boost ClpC unfolding activity in absence of adaptor without altering general substrate specificity.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data showing specific degradation of GFP-SsrA but not GFP-SsrA-DD.

claim: B. subtilis ClpC activation by adaptors involves strong stimulation of ClpC ATPase activity.
source: B. subtilis ClpC activation by adaptors involves strong stimulation of ClpC ATPase activity (Turgay et al., 1997; Mei et al., 2009; Persuh et al., 1999), which we confirm here for S. aureus ClpC and MecA (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work and experimental data in Figure 2A.

claim: ClpC WT exhibits a very low basal ATPase activity (0.4 ATP/min/monomer).
source: ClpC WT exhibits a very low basal ATPase activity (0.4 ATP/min/monomer), rationalizing its poor standalone degradation activity.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: All activated MD mutants (F436A, R443A, ΔM) exhibited strongly increased basal ATPase activities (3.3–5.4 ATP/min/monomer).
source: Notably, all activated MD mutants (F436A, R443A, ΔM) exhibited strongly increased basal ATPase activities (3.3–5.4 ATP/min/monomer) that were further increased by substrate casein (1.64–2.47-fold stimulation) in contrast to ClpC WT (Figure 2A/B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A/B.

claim: Basal ATPase activities of ClpC MD mutants were further increased by substrate casein (1.64–2.47-fold stimulation).
source: Notably, all activated MD mutants (F436A, R443A, ΔM) exhibited strongly increased basal ATPase activities (3.3–5.4 ATP/min/monomer) that were further increased by substrate casein (1.64–2.47-fold stimulation) in contrast to ClpC WT (Figure 2A/B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A/B.

claim: Casein-stimulated ClpC MD mutants reached 33% of total ATPase activity determined for MecA-activated ClpC WT.
source: Casein-stimulated ClpC MD mutants reached 33% of total ATPase activity determined for MecA-activated ClpC WT.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2.

claim: N-domain deletion increased basal ATPase activity of ΔN-ClpC.
source: N-domain deletion also increased basal ATPase activity of ΔN-ClpC.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Combining ΔN-ClpC with M-domain mutants had an additive stimulatory effect on ATPase activities.
source: Combining ΔN-ClpC with M-domain mutants had an additive stimulatory effect on ATPase activities, suggesting that the underlying mechanisms are distinct from one another (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A and inference about distinct mechanisms.

claim: Increased basal ATPase activities of ClpC MD mutants can explain adaptor-independent substrate degradation.
source: We infer increased basal ATPase activities of ClpC MD mutants (in context of fullength ClpC and ΔN-ClpC) can explain adaptor-independent substrate degradation.
evidence: This is an inference based on the correlation between ATPase activity and degradation activity.

claim: ATPase activation alone is not sufficient to explain ClpC activation as ΔN-ClpC did not allow degradation of GFP-SsrA despite having increased basal ATPase activity.
source: However, ATPase activation alone is not sufficient to explain ClpC activation as ΔN-ClpC did not allow degradation of GFP-SsrA despite having increased basal ATPase activity.
evidence: This is an inference based on comparing ATPase activity and degradation activity data.

claim: The cryo-EM structure of S. aureus ClpC without MecA was solved at 8.4 Å resolution using ~90,000 collected particles.
source: The structure of ClpC on its own was solved at 8.4 Å resolution using ~90.000 collected particles (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by the cryo-EM data and methods described.

claim: ClpC without MecA assumes a conformation different from the canonical hexameric arrangement of AAA+ proteins.
source: Surprisingly, raw images and subsequent 2D classification revealed immediately that ClpC assumes a conformation different from the canonical hexameric arrangement of AAA+ proteins (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A/B).
evidence: This is supported by cryo-EM data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A/B.

claim: ClpC without MecA assembles into an oligomeric assembly made of two open spirals that interact via head-to-head contacts mainly mediated by the MDs.
source: Indeed, reconstructions revealed that ClpC without MecA assembles into an oligomeric assembly made of two open spirals that interact via head-to-head contacts mainly mediated by the MDs (Figure 3A/B, Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by cryo-EM reconstruction data shown in Figure 3A/B and Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: ClpC half spirals have inter-subunit interfaces similar to the crystal structure of Hsp104 (PDB code: 5d4w).
source: More specifically, ClpC half spirals have inter-subunit interfaces similar to the crystal structure of Hsp104 (PDB code: 5d4w) (Heuck et al., 2016) and the EM map of Hsp104 in complex with ADP (PDB code: 5vy8) (Gates et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a comparison to known structures supported by citations to Heuck et al., 2016 and Gates et al., 2017.

claim: ClpC forms a double spiral that is open on one side resulting in a cradle-like molecule.
source: ClpC did not form a half spiral but a double spiral that is open on one side (Figure 3A/B, Figure 3—figure supplement 1A/B, Figure 3—video 1) resulting in a cradle-like molecule with the peripheral subunits more mobile than the core ones, as shown by lower local resolution (Figure 3—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This is supported by cryo-EM data shown in Figure 3A/B and related figures.

claim: Peripheral ClpC subunits are more mobile than the core ones, as shown by lower local resolution.
source: ClpC did not form a half spiral but a double spiral that is open on one side (Figure 3A/B, Figure 3—figure supplement 1A/B, Figure 3—video 1) resulting in a cradle-like molecule with the peripheral subunits more mobile than the core ones, as shown by lower local resolution (Figure 3—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This is supported by local resolution analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2A.

claim: The MDs coiled-coils constitute the backbone of the spiral and mediate the spiral head-to-head contacts.
source: The MDs coiled-coils constitute the backbone of the spiral and mediate the spiral head-to-head contacts, which involve residues F436, R443 and D444 providing a structural rationale for the activated states of respective MD mutants (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is supported by structural analysis shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Head-to-head MD contacts involve residues F436, R443 and D444.
source: The MDs coiled-coils constitute the backbone of the spiral and mediate the spiral head-to-head contacts, which involve residues F436, R443 and D444 providing a structural rationale for the activated states of respective MD mutants (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is supported by structural analysis shown in Figure 3D.

claim: The MD-MD head-to-head interaction stops the formation of virtually infinite spirals allowing the formation of a compact, repressed ClpC reservoir.
source: The MD-MD head-to-head interaction stops the formation of virtually infinite spirals as in the Hsp104 crystal arrangements allowing the formation of a compact, repressed ClpC reservoir.
evidence: This is an inference based on the structural data and comparison to Hsp104.

claim: The helical ClpC assembly is a dynamic inactive resting state which will interfere with substrate binding, association of the ClpP peptidase and interaction with adaptor proteins.
source: We envision the helical ClpC assembly as a dynamic inactive resting state, which will interfere with substrate binding, association of the ClpP peptidase and interaction with adaptor proteins.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation based on the structural data.

claim: The S. aureus ClpC-MecA cryo-EM map was reconstructed at 11 Å resolution with ~26,000 particles.
source: The S. aureus ClpC-MecA cryo-EM map was reconstructed at 11 Å resolution with ~26,000 particles, (Figure 3—figure supplement 3A–D) and shows the classical hexameric assembly previously described (Wang et al., 2011; Liu et al., 2013), with MecA interacting with both the MD and the N-domain of ClpC (Figure 3E).
evidence: This is supported by cryo-EM data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3A–D.

claim: The ClpC-MecA structure shows the classical hexameric assembly previously described.
source: The S. aureus ClpC-MecA cryo-EM map was reconstructed at 11 Å resolution with ~26,000 particles, (Figure 3—figure supplement 3A–D) and shows the classical hexameric assembly previously described (Wang et al., 2011; Liu et al., 2013), with MecA interacting with both the MD and the N-domain of ClpC (Figure 3E).
evidence: This is supported by cryo-EM data and citations to Wang et al., 2011; Liu et al., 2013.

claim: MecA interacts with both the MD and the N-domain of ClpC.
source: The S. aureus ClpC-MecA cryo-EM map was reconstructed at 11 Å resolution with ~26,000 particles, (Figure 3—figure supplement 3A–D) and shows the classical hexameric assembly previously described (Wang et al., 2011; Liu et al., 2013), with MecA interacting with both the MD and the N-domain of ClpC (Figure 3E).
evidence: This is supported by cryo-EM data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: From the resting to the MecA-bound state the N-domains undergo a 45° rotation that repositions the MecA-binding loop region.
source: From the resting to the MecA-bound state the N-domains undergo a 45° rotation that repositions the MecA-binding loop region from being blocked by the MD of the neighbouring subunit to be available and engaged in MecA binding (Figure 3—figure supplement 3E/F).
evidence: This is supported by structural comparison shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3E/F.

claim: Binding of MecA to MDs breaks head-to-head MD contacts and is expected to prevent formation of the ClpC resting state.
source: Additionally, binding of MecA to MDs breaks head-to-head MD contacts and is therefore expected to prevent formation of the ClpC resting state.
evidence: This is an inference based on the structural data showing MecA binding to MD sites.

claim: The structures of ClpC alone or in complex with MecA show a dramatic reorganization from a helical resting state to a planar canonical AAA+ hexamer.
source: Taken together, our structures of ClpC alone or in complex with MecA show a dramatic reorganization from a helical resting state to a planar canonical AAA+ hexamer, explaining ClpC activation by the adaptor MecA.
evidence: This is a summary inference based on the cryo-EM structural data.

claim: Intermolecular head-to-head contacts of MDs form the backbone of the ClpC resting state, qualifying the MD as crucial negative regulatory element.
source: Intermolecular head-to-head contacts of MDs form the backbone of the ClpC resting state, qualifying the MD as crucial negative regulatory element consistent with MD mutant characterization.
evidence: This is an inference based on structural data and mutant characterization.

claim: ClpC-C311T/E437C and ClpC-C311T/E435C were active in MecA-dependent protein degradation under reducing conditions.
source: ClpC-C311T/E435C and ClpC-C311T/E437C were active in MecA-dependent protein degradation under reducing conditions (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Formation of crosslink products under oxidizing conditions was observed for ClpC-C311T/E437C but not for ClpC-C311T/E435C and the ClpC-C311T control.
source: Formation of crosslink products under oxidizing conditions that were fully reverted by addition of reducing agent was observed for ClpC-C311T/E437C but not for ClpC-C311T/E435C and the ClpC-C311T control (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B.

claim: E437 residues of two interacting M-domains are facing one another while E435 residues are oriented in opposite directions.
source: This documents specificity of disulfide crosslinking and agrees well with the ClpC resting state model, showing E437 residues of two interacting M-domains are facing one another while E435 residues are oriented in opposite directions (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by structural model shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B.

claim: E437C disulfide crosslinking was most efficient in absence of nucleotide or presence of ADP and ATP, and less efficient in presence of ATPγS.
source: E437C disulfide crosslinking was most efficient in absence of nucleotide or presence of ADP and ATP, and less efficient in presence of ATPγS (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1C.

claim: ClpC-E437C crosslinking in presence of MecA was strongly reduced.
source: Importantly, ClpC-E437C crosslinking in presence of MecA was strongly reduced (Figure 4A), consistent with MecA binding to MDs preventing head-to-head MD interactions.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Crosslinking efficiency was reduced for ClpC-F436A/E437C, indicating a crucial contribution of F436 to intermolecular MD contacts.
source: Similarly, crosslinking efficiency was reduced for ClpC-F436A/E437C, indicating a crucial contribution of F436 to intermolecular MD contacts (Figure 4B), consistent with the ClpC WT cryo-EM structure.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: ClpC-DWB was crosslinked to very large assemblies that were just entering the separating gel in SDS-PAGE in absence and presence of ATP.
source: ClpC-DWB was crosslinked to very large assemblies that were just entering the separating gel in SDS-PAGE in absence and presence of ATP (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Addition of MecA allowed for formation of a smaller high molecular weight complex similar in size to crosslinked ClpB hexamers.
source: Addition of MecA allowed for formation of a smaller high molecular weight complex similar in size to crosslinked ClpB hexamers that were used as reference (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: ClpC-F436A-DWB stayed monomeric in absence of nucleotide, indicating that large assemblies observed for ClpC-DWB rely entirely on MD contacts.
source: ClpC-F436A-DWB stayed monomeric in absence of nucleotide, indicating that large assemblies observed for ClpC-DWB rely entirely on MD contacts (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5A and inference about MD dependence.

claim: ClpC-F436A-DWB crosslinking in presence of ATP caused formation of defined ClpC-F436A-DWB complexes that were similar in size to crosslinked ClpB hexamers.
source: ClpC-F436A-DWB crosslinking in presence of ATP caused formation of defined ClpC-F436A-DWB complexes that were similar in size to crosslinked ClpB hexamers.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: In absence of nucleotide ΔN-ClpC stayed monomeric, suggesting that N-domain contacts to AAA-1 contribute to assembly formation.
source: In absence of nucleotide ΔN-ClpC stayed monomeric, suggesting that N-domain contacts to AAA-1 contribute to assembly formation.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5B and inference about N-domain contribution.

claim: In presence of ATPγS, ΔN-ClpC was still crosslinked to high molecular weight complexes larger than ClpB hexamers indicating N-domains are not essential for resting state formation.
source: However, in presence of ATPγS, ΔN-ClpC was still crosslinked to high molecular weight complexes larger than ClpB hexamers indicating N-domains are not essential for resting state formation whereas nucleotide binding to AAA domains is crucial (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: ΔN-ClpC-F436A (+ATPγS) was predominantly crosslinked to hexamers, demonstrating the unique and dominant role of MDs in controlling resting state formation.
source: ΔN-ClpC-F436A (+ATPγS) was predominantly crosslinked to hexamers, demonstrating the unique and dominant role of MDs in controlling resting state formation.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: In absence of ATP ClpC-DWB showed a broad elution profile, suggesting formation of variable assemblies ranging from monomers to hexamers.
source: In absence of ATP ClpC-DWB showed a broad elution profile, suggesting formation of variable assemblies ranging from monomers to hexamers.
evidence: This is supported by size exclusion chromatography data shown in Figure 5C and Figure 5—figure supplement 2A.

claim: ATP addition caused formation of larger ClpC assemblies that eluted prior to ClpB hexamers and a 670 kDa standard protein.
source: ATP addition caused formation of larger ClpC assemblies that eluted prior to ClpB hexamers and a 670 kDa standard protein, suggesting formation of ClpC complexes larger than hexamers (Figure 5C, Figure 5—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This is supported by size exclusion chromatography data shown in Figure 5C and Figure 5—figure supplement 2A.

claim: Static light scattering measurements revealed a molecular mass of ≈ 956 kDa for ClpC-DWB + ATP corresponding to a decameric complex.
source: This was confirmed by static light scattering (SLS) measurements, revealing a molecular mass of ≈ 956 kDa corresponding to a decameric complex, consistent with cryoEM analysis (Figure 5—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This is supported by SLS data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2B.

claim: Presence of MecA sharpened the ClpC elution profile and shifted ClpC-DWB fractions to later elution volumes overlapping with ClpB hexamers.
source: Presence of MecA sharpened the ClpC elution profile and shifted ClpC-DWB fractions to later elution volumes right after the 670 kDa standard protein and now overlapping with ClpB hexamers (Figure 5C, Figure 5—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This is supported by size exclusion chromatography data shown in Figure 5C and Figure 5—figure supplement 2A.

claim: MecA binding shifts ClpC from a large, non-hexameric assembly to a ClpC6/MecA6 complex.
source: This indicates that MecA binding shifts ClpC from a large, non-hexameric assembly to a ClpC6/MecA6 complex.
evidence: This is an inference based on size exclusion chromatography and SLS data.

claim: ClpC-DWB-F436A eluted as defined species right at the elution volume of a 158 kDa standard protein in absence of ATP suggesting formation of monomers/dimers.
source: In absence of ATP the MD mutant eluted as defined species right at the elution volume of a 158 kDa standard protein suggesting formation of monomers/dimers (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is supported by size exclusion chromatography data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: ClpC-DWB-F436A showed a broad elution profile upon ATP addition.
source: Unexpectedly, ClpC-DWB-F436A showed a broad elution profile upon ATP addition.
evidence: This is supported by size exclusion chromatography data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Autodegradation of ClpC-F436A, ClpC-R443A and ClpC-ΔM but not ClpC WT was observed in presence of ClpP.
source: Indeed, we observed autodegradation of ClpC-F436A, ClpC-R443A and ClpC-ΔM but not ClpC WT in presence of ClpP (Figure 5—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 3.

claim: Presence of casein sharpened the ClpC-DWB-F436A elution profile that was comparable to ClpC-DWB/MecA complexes and distinct from ClpC-DWB, suggesting hexamer formation.
source: Presence of casein sharpened the ClpC-DWB-F436A elution profile that was comparable to ClpC-DWB/MecA complexes and distinct from ClpC-DWB, suggesting hexamer formation, which was confirmed by mass determination by SLS (587 kDa) (Figure 5C, Figure 5—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This is supported by size exclusion chromatography and SLS data shown in Figure 5C and Figure 5—figure supplement 2B.

claim: 2D classification of ClpC-F436A with casein and ATPγS indicates that ClpC-F436A assembles in a hexamer similar to ClpC WT with MecA.
source: To further prove ClpC-F436A hexamer formation, a small cryo-EM dataset of ClpC-F436A with casein and ATPγS was collected and analyzed via 2D classification. Classes indicate that the ClpC-F436A assembles in an hexamer similar to ClpC WT with MecA (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is supported by cryo-EM 2D classification data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: ClpC-DWB forms large, non-hexameric assemblies in a MD dependent manner.
source: Together our findings demonstrate that ClpC-DWB forms large, non-hexameric assemblies in a MD dependent manner, supporting the derived ClpC WT cryo-EM structure.
evidence: This is a summary inference based on crosslinking and size exclusion chromatography data.

claim: The large ClpC-DWB assembly does not allow for efficient substrate binding or association with the ClpP peptidase.
source: This large ClpC-DWB assembly should neither allow for efficient substrate binding nor association with the ClpP peptidase. This prediction was confirmed by size exclusion chromatography showing poor interaction with ClpP and negligible binding to substrate FITC-casein (Figure 5E, Figure 5—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: This is supported by size exclusion chromatography data shown in Figure 5E and Figure 5—figure supplement 2C.

claim: Efficient binding to FITC-casein and ClpP was observed upon addition of MecA and for ClpC-DWB-F436A (- MecA).
source: In contrast, efficient binding to FITC-casein and ClpP was observed upon addition of MecA and for ClpC-DWB-F436A (- MecA) (Figure 5E, Figure 5—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: This is supported by size exclusion chromatography data shown in Figure 5E and Figure 5—figure supplement 2C.

claim: Expression of ΔN-ClpC-F436A was highly toxic at all temperatures tested.
source: We observed strong toxicity upon expression of ΔN-ClpC-F436A at all temperatures tested while ClpC-F436A expression became lethal at 37°C and 40°C (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is supported by spot test data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: ClpC-F436A expression became lethal at 37°C and 40°C.
source: We observed strong toxicity upon expression of ΔN-ClpC-F436A at all temperatures tested while ClpC-F436A expression became lethal at 37°C and 40°C (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is supported by spot test data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Toxicity of ClpC MD mutants was much higher as compared to ClpC-WT and ΔN-ClpC, suggesting an essential cellular need for ClpC repression by MDs.
source: Toxicity of ClpC MD mutants was much higher as compared to ClpC-WT and ΔN-ClpC, suggesting an essential cellular need for ClpC repression by MDs.
evidence: This is an inference based on comparing toxicity data.

claim: Toxicity of ClpC MD mutants was dependent on coexpression of S. aureus ClpP.
source: Furthermore, toxicity of ClpC MD mutants was dependent on coexpression of S. aureus ClpP, suggesting that uncontrolled protein degradation caused by constitutively activation results in cell death (Figure 6—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by spot test data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Expression of clpC-F436A but not clpC wt in presence of 100 μM IPTG was highly toxic to B. subtilis cells at all temperatures (30–50°C).
source: Expression of clpC-F436A but not clpC wt in presence of 100 μM IPTG was highly toxic at all temperatures (30–50°C) (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is supported by spot test data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Growth of clpC::tet cells was not impaired, demonstrating that toxicity of ClpC-F436A reflects a gain-of-function phenotype.
source: Importantly, growth of clpC::tet cells was not impaired, demonstrating that toxicity of ClpC-F436A reflects a gain-of-function phenotype and is not caused by loss of adaptor interaction (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is supported by spot test data shown in Figure 6B and inference about gain-of-function.

claim: F436 and R443, identified as key MD residues in ClpC activity control, are largely conserved in ClpE and ClpL M-domains.
source: Notably, F436 and R443, identified here as key MD residues in ClpC activity control, are largely conserved in ClpE and ClpL M-domains (Figure 6C).
evidence: This is supported by sequence alignment shown in Figure 6C.

claim: Expression of clpE-Y344A but not clpE wt in presence of 100 μM IPTG was highly toxic to B. subtilis cells at all temperatures tested (30–50°C).
source: Expression of clpE-Y344A but not clpE wt in presence of 100 μM IPTG was highly toxic to B. subtilis cells at all temperatures tested (30–50°C) (Figure 6D).
evidence: This is supported by spot test data shown in Figure 6D.

claim: ClpE MDs are essential to downregulate ClpE activity preventing cellular toxicity.
source: This suggests that ClpE MDs are also essential to downregulate ClpE activity preventing cellular toxicity.
evidence: This is an inference based on the toxicity data for ClpE-Y344A mutant.

claim: ClpC MDs function as molecular switches, ensuring repression in the ground state and allowing for activation in presence of substrate recruiting adaptors.
source: Thereby ClpC MDs function as molecular switches, similar to ClpB/Hsp104 MDs, ensuring repression in the ground state and allowing for activation in presence of substrate recruiting adaptors (Figure 7).
evidence: This is a summary inference based on all the structural and biochemical data.

claim: F436 is essential for both intermolecular MD interaction and MecA binding.
source: This dual activity is best illustrated for MD residue F436 located at the tip of the coiled-coil structure. F436 is essential for both, intermolecular MD interaction and MecA binding (Figure 7).
evidence: This is supported by structural and biochemical data throughout the manuscript.

claim: The interaction surface of MDs is limited (50 Å2).
source: The interaction surface of MDs is limited (50 Å2) which has implications on the stability of the resting state complex.
evidence: This is based on structural analysis of the MD-MD interface.

claim: Multiple MD contacts provide sufficient stickiness to stabilize a resting state core, while providing dynamics to peripheral subunits.
source: We speculate that multiple MD contacts provide sufficient stickiness to stabilize a resting state core, while providing dynamics to peripheral subunits, in agreement with our structural and biochemical analysis.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation based on structural and biochemical data.

claim: ClpC subunit dissociation is prerequisite for MecA binding.
source: As MecA-binding sites in N- and M-domains are not accessible in the resting state, we suggest that ClpC subunit dissociation is prerequisite for MecA binding.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation based on the structural data.

claim: Sequestering inactive ClpC subunits in a resting state structure might provide better protection against non-specific interactions with other cellular components or degradation by proteases as compared to freely accessible monomers.
source: Sequestering inactive ClpC subunits in a resting state structure might provide better protection against non-specific interactions with other cellular components or degradation by proteases as compared to freely accessible monomers.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation about the functional advantage of the resting state.

claim: Former ClpC analysis was performed in presence of high salt concentrations (300 mM NaCl), which likely interfere with MD head-to-head contacts involving charged residues (R443, D444).
source: We realize that former ClpC analysis was performed in presence of high salt concentrations (300 mM NaCl), which likely interfere with MD head-to-head contacts involving charged residues (R443, D444).
evidence: This is an inference about why previous studies showed different results.

claim: Adaptor proteins target themselves for degradation by ClpC/ClpP if substrates are no longer available.
source: Adaptor proteins are targeting themselves for degradation by ClpC/ClpP if substrates are no longer available (Mei et al., 2009; Turgay et al., 1998; Kirstein et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Mei et al., 2009; Turgay et al., 1998; Kirstein et al., 2007.

claim: This mechanism couples substrate availability with ClpC activation and ensures fast ClpC inactivation in absence of substrate.
source: This mechanism couples substrate availability with ClpC activation and ensures fast ClpC inactivation in absence of substrate by causing dissociation of ClpC hexamers into monomers that are subsequently sequestered in the resting state.
evidence: This is an inference about the regulatory mechanism.

claim: The Hsp70 member BIP forms large, inactive resting states that are converted into active species depending on substrate availability.
source: Notably, other chaperone machineries including the Hsp70 member BIP (Preissler et al., 2015) and the AAA+ protein Rca (Mueller-Cajar et al., 2011) also form large, inactive resting states that are converted into active species depending on substrate availability.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Preissler et al., 2015 and Mueller-Cajar et al., 2011.

claim: The AAA+ protein Rca forms large, inactive resting states that are converted into active species depending on substrate availability.
source: Notably, other chaperone machineries including the Hsp70 member BIP (Preissler et al., 2015) and the AAA+ protein Rca (Mueller-Cajar et al., 2011) also form large, inactive resting states that are converted into active species depending on substrate availability.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Preissler et al., 2015 and Mueller-Cajar et al., 2011.

claim: Constitutively activated ClpC MD mutants exert strong toxicity in E. coli and B. subtilis cells, demonstrating an essential physiological need to tightly control ClpC function.
source: Constitutively activated ClpC MD mutants exert strong toxicity in E. coli and B. subtilis cells, demonstrating an essential physiological need to tightly control ClpC function.
evidence: This is a summary inference based on the toxicity data in Figure 6.

claim: Adapters confer a higher degree of substrate specificity to ClpC as compared to activated ClpC MD mutants.
source: This suggests that adapters confer a higher degree of substrate specificity to ClpC as compared to activated ClpC MD mutants.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that ClpC WT with adapters is not toxic while MD mutants are toxic.

claim: Mistargeted protein degradation by deregulated ClpC MD mutants leads to cell death.
source: We assume that mistargeted protein degradation by deregulated ClpC MD mutants of e.g. newly synthesized proteins or secretory proteins, which did not yet reach their native structures or cellular compartment, leads to cell death.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation about the mechanism of toxicity.

claim: Homologous MDs are present in the AAA+ protein family members ClpE and ClpL and key residues driving formation of the ClpC resting state are evolutionary conserved.
source: Homologous MDs are present in the AAA+ protein family members ClpE and ClpL and key residues driving formation of the ClpC resting state are evolutionary conserved.
evidence: This is supported by sequence alignment data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: The repressing mode of MDs established for ClpC is also operational in ClpE and ClpL and thus is a more general mechanism for controlling bacterial AAA+ chaperone systems.
source: We show that mutating a key regulatory MD residue of ClpE also causes cellular toxicity, strongly suggesting that the repressing mode of MDs established here for ClpC is also operational in ClpE and ClpL and thus is a more general mechanism for controlling bacterial AAA+ chaperone systems.
evidence: This is an inference based on the ClpE toxicity data and sequence conservation.

claim: Severe toxicity of ClpC and ClpE MD mutants qualifies these AAA+ chaperones as targets for antimicrobials.
source: Severe toxicity of ClpC and ClpE MD mutants qualifies these AAA+ chaperones as targets for antimicrobials.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation about potential applications.

claim: The M. tuberculosis ClpC N-terminal domain was recently identified as target of cyclic peptides with antibacterial activities.
source: Notably, the M. tuberculosis ClpC N-terminal domain was recently identified as target of cyclic peptides with antibacterial activities (Schmitt et al., 2011; Gao et al., 2015; Gavrish et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Schmitt et al., 2011; Gao et al., 2015; Gavrish et al., 2014.

claim: The findings identify MDs as crucial regulatory elements and thus drug targets offering a promising approach to attack multi-drug resistant bacteria.
source: Our findings presented here open a new route for toxic ClpC deregulation by identifying MDs as crucial regulatory elements and thus drug targets and offering a promising approach to attack multi-drug resistant bacteria.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation about potential applications.
